c.tagline: River meets ocean at Africa's smallest mainland capital.

taxi.fareNote: Tourist taxis (green) charge fixed negotiated fares set by tourism board tariffs; yellow-yellow local shared taxis are cheaper but follow fixed routes rather than meters. Always agree the fare before departure as meters are not used.

emergency.note: Response times can be slow; many hotels and resorts keep private clinic contacts and expats often rely on Medicare/Westfield or Kairaba clinics in Kotu/Fajara for faster service.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

hood_desc: The historic colonial-era capital on St Mary's Island itself, with faded colonial architecture, Albert Market, and government buildings; few tourists actually sleep here, suiting history buffs and those wanting an authentic, non-touristy base near the ferry terminal.

The Gambia's main beach resort strip with Kololi, Senegambia and Bijilo blending together; big all-inclusive resorts, nightlife, restaurants and craft markets, suiting first-time visitors and package travelers who want beach plus amenities in one place.

A quieter beachfront area with a mix of package hotels and self-catering apartments just north of Kololi, popular with British and European charter tourists and families wanting a calmer beach scene with easy access to Senegambia's nightlife.

An upscale, leafy residential and diplomatic area near the coast with boutique lodges, embassies and golf course, suiting travelers wanting a quieter, more refined stay close to the beach and Cape Point.

A fishing village atmosphere at the northern tip of the peninsula where the river meets the Atlantic, home to a monkey sanctuary and craft markets, suiting travelers who want a laid-back, semi-local coastal vibe.

water.note: Tap water is not safe; use sealed bottled water only.

transit.pay: Pay cash in dalasi directly to the driver or conductor on boarding for buses and bush taxis; fares for shared routes are fixed per seat and posted at motor parks. The Banjul-Barra ferry sells paper tickets at the terminal for foot passengers and vehicles.
transit.hours: Bush taxis and gelly-gellys run roughly 6am-8pm with no fixed schedule (depart when full); GTSC buses run limited daytime schedules; the Banjul-Barra ferry operates several crossings daily but with unpredictable delays and no reliable night service.
transit.note: There is no formal urban transit network; public transport is dominated by informal shared taxis and minibuses, and most visitors rely on hotel transfers or negotiated taxis instead.

bus: private minivan/gelly-gelly bush taxis between Banjul, Serekunda and Kombo coastal towns
ferry: Banjul-Barra Ferry across the River Gambia

tip.r: Not obligatory but appreciated in resorts and restaurants; rounding up or 10% is common for good service, especially where a service charge isn't already included.

food.name: Benachin
food.desc: The Gambian one-pot: rice cooked in a tomato and fish or meat broth with cassava, aubergine and pumpkin. Its Wolof name means one pot.

places.name: Albert Market food stalls
places.note: Women ladle benachin from cast-iron pots near the old clock tower from mid-morning.

places.name: John Raymond's Restaurant
places.note: Long-standing local kitchen praised for its benachin and yassa.

places.name: Madeleine's Kitchen
places.note: Home-style Gambian cooking with a rotating daily pot and generous portions.

food.name: Domoda
food.desc: Thick groundnut stew, peanut paste cooked down with tomato, pumpkin and beef, chicken or fish, poured over white rice; the national comfort dish.

places.name: Albert Market food stalls
places.note: Cheapest and best domoda in the capital, eaten standing at the stall.

places.name: Ali Baba
places.note: Reliable spot for Gambian staples served in a busy, informal dining room.

places.name: Mr Bass
places.note: Community restaurant with a broad Gambian menu and occasional live bands.

food.name: Yassa
food.desc: Chicken or fish marinated in lemon, mustard and chilli then grilled and smothered in a mountain of slow-cooked onions, served with rice.

places.name: John Raymond's Restaurant
places.note: Singled out locally for its yassa; a dependable sit-down option in the capital.

places.name: Madeleine's Kitchen
places.note: Fish yassa made with the day's catch and properly caramelised onions.

places.name: Albert Market food stalls
places.note: Market cooks serve yassa at lunch alongside benachin and domoda.

food.name: Superkanja
food.desc: Okra stew thickened with palm oil, smoked fish and beef, cooked until glossy and rich; a heavier, more traditional plate than the tourist-menu dishes.

places.name: Albert Market food stalls
places.note: Made in bulk for market traders; ask which pot is superkanja before it runs out.

places.name: Madeleine's Kitchen
places.note: Keeps the heavier traditional stews on the menu, not just the familiar dishes.

places.name: Serrekunda Market food stalls
places.note: The Gambia's biggest market, with dozens of cooks turning out okra and leaf stews.

food.name: Tapalapa Bread
food.desc: Dense wood-fired baguette of millet, maize and wheat flour, split and filled with fried fish, bean akara or ebbeh for breakfast.

places.name: Albert Market food stalls
places.note: Sold hot from morning carts and filled to order with akara or fish.

places.name: Half Die street vendors
places.note: Neighbourhood bakeries and breakfast carts serving tapalapa from dawn.

places.name: Serrekunda Market food stalls
places.note: Bread stands ring the market; the queue tells you which oven is best.

food.name: Grilled Fish and Afra
food.desc: Bonga, ladyfish or barracuda grilled over charcoal, or afra, chunks of grilled meat served in bread with onions, mustard and chilli.

places.name: Bakau Fish Market
places.note: Buy from the boats and have it grilled on the spot at the beachside pits.

places.name: Mr Bass
places.note: Seaside kitchen doing whole grilled fish with local sauces.

places.name: Albert Market food stalls
places.note: Charcoal afra grills fire up in the late afternoon around the market edges.

food.name: Wonjo
food.desc: Deep red hibiscus infusion sweetened and chilled, sometimes spiked with ginger or mint; sold in frozen sachets on every street. Non-alcoholic.

places.name: Albert Market food stalls
places.note: Vendors sell wonjo in chilled sachets and bottles throughout the market.

places.name: Serrekunda Market food stalls
places.note: Made fresh in large containers and poured by the cup for a few dalasi.

places.name: Bakau Fish Market
places.note: Drinks sellers work the fish market and beach with wonjo and baobab juice.

food.name: Bouye
food.desc: Baobab fruit juice: the chalky white pulp soaked in water with milk and sugar into a tart, creamy drink. Non-alcoholic and full of vitamin C.

places.name: Albert Market food stalls
places.note: Sold alongside wonjo in bags and bottles; the baobab pods are on sale nearby.

places.name: Serrekunda Market food stalls
places.note: Fresh bouye mixed daily by juice vendors in the market's food aisles.

places.name: Madeleine's Kitchen
places.note: Serves house-made bouye and wonjo with its Gambian plates.

food.name: Attaya
food.desc: Strong Chinese gunpowder green tea brewed over coals and poured from height into small glasses in three ever-sweeter rounds. Non-alcoholic.

places.name: Half Die street corners
places.note: Attaya circles form on the pavement all day; being invited to sit is the point.

places.name: Albert Market food stalls
places.note: Traders brew attaya between customers and sell glasses to passers-by.

places.name: Bakau Fish Market
places.note: Fishermen keep attaya pots going on the beach while waiting on the tide.

landmarks: Arch 22

This towering monument, built to commemorate the 1994 coup, is Banjul's most recognizable landmark and offers panoramic city views from its observation deck. Its bold, modern silhouette dominates the skyline.
Albert Market

One of West Africa's most vibrant markets, packed with stalls selling colorful fabrics, spices, jewelry, and crafts. The sensory overload of sights and sounds makes it an unmissable Banjul experience.
King Fahad Mosque
An elegant, Saudi-funded mosque with gleaming minarets that serves as one of the country's major centers of worship. Its clean lines and scale make it a striking photographic subject.
National Museum of The Gambia
This compact but engaging museum traces Gambian history from precolonial kingdoms through the slave trade to independence. It's an essential stop for understanding the nation's story.
McCarthy Square
A leafy public square at the center of Banjul, lined with historic buildings and used for parades and national events. It's a pleasant spot to pause and watch daily city life unfold.
Cathedral of Our Lady of the Assumption
A modest but charming Catholic cathedral reflecting Banjul's colonial-era architecture. Its quiet courtyard offers a peaceful contrast to the busy streets nearby.
State House
The official residence of The Gambia's president, an elegant colonial-era building overlooking the harbor. Its guards and stately grounds make it a notable photo stop on a walking tour.
Banjul Waterfront and Harbour
Watch fishing pirogues and ferries crossing the mouth of the Gambia River, with Barra visible across the water. Sunset here paints the sky and water in brilliant color.
Denton Bridge
This causeway linking Banjul to the mainland is known for its mangrove-lined creeks and as a launch point for river tours. Birdwatchers often stop here to spot herons and kingfishers.
Katchikally Crocodile Pool
Just outside the city in Bakau, this sacred pool lets visitors get remarkably close to dozens of resident Nile crocodiles. It's one of the most memorable wildlife encounters near the capital.

train.note: The Gambia has no railway. The only lines it ever had were short hand-worked tramways serving the wharves at Bathurst (now Banjul), Kuntaur and Kaur in colonial times, and they had all disappeared by the 1960s; nothing has been built since. Senegal's Dakar-Tambacounda railway comes nowhere near the border and is itself largely out of passenger service, so there is no rail option in or out. Every overland journey is by road or across the river.

bus.note: Most cross-border travel is in shared sept-place Peugeots and minibuses rather than scheduled coaches: from Banjul you take the Barra ferry and pick up transport on the north bank at Barra for the Senegalese border at Karang and on to Dakar, five to seven hours in all with the crossings, or go via the Senegambia bridge at Farafenni if you are heading upriver or to the Casamance. Senegal's state operator Dakar Dem Dikk has extended scheduled services into the sub-region under its Africa Dem Dikk arm. Inside the country, GTSC coaches and gelly-gelly minibuses leave from the Banjul terminal near the ferry ramp for Serekunda, Soma, Farafenni and Basse Santa Su, with fares paid on board; allow a full day for the trip upriver.

intl.to: Barra (Gambia) - from the Banjul ferry terminal at the north end of Liberation Avenue, ~35-45 min across the river mouth
intl.op: Gambia Ports Authority ferry service — tickets at the terminal

ferry.note: The Banjul-Barra ferry is the main link between the south and north banks of the River Gambia and the usual first leg of any journey towards Senegal's Sine-Saloum; the terminal is at the end of Liberation Avenue, walking distance from Albert Market. Crossings take 35-45 minutes when the boats are running, but the service is notoriously unreliable - vessels go out of service for long periods, vehicle queues can last hours and foot passengers board first, which is why many drivers use the Senegambia bridge at Farafenni instead. There are no international ferry services; upriver villages are served informally by pirogues, and river cruises are tourist charters rather than transport.
